slides.0.title: Understanding Brandy
slides.0.subtitle: Definition, name origin and history from Dutch traders to the French regions
slides.1.title: Name and definition
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Where the name comes from
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Brandy comes from Dutch brandewijn, literally "burnt wine"; English recorded brandy-wine in the 1620s and the short form brandy in the 1650s; German Branntwein shares the origin (etymonline)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: The basic idea
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Distilling finished wine and ageing it in oak gives grape brandy; distillation concentrates alcohol and aroma, and ageing adds colour and complexity
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Scope of this course
slides.1.highlights.2.content: This course focuses on grape brandy (Cognac, Armagnac, Brandy de Jerez, Metaxa, Pisco, Grappa and others); Calvados and other fruit brandies are outside its scope
slides.1.content: The word itself describes the method: heating wine.
slides.2.title: The EU legal definition
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Thresholds for Brandy / Weinbrand
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Regulation (EU) 2019/787, Annex I: at least 36% vol at bottling; at least 1 year in oak vessels of 1,000 L or more, or 6 months in oak casks under 1,000 L
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Compositional limits
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Volatile substances at least 125 g per hl of pure alcohol, methanol at most 200 g per hl, added sugar (as invert sugar) at most 35 g/L; only caramel may be used, for colour, and no alcohol may be added
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Related categories
slides.2.highlights.2.content: The same annex also lists Wine spirit (at least 37.5%, distilled below 86% vol), Grape marc spirit (at least 37.5%) and Raisin spirit (at least 37.5%, from dried Corinth Black or Moscatel of Alexandria grapes)
slides.2.content: Individual appellations such as Cognac and Armagnac add stricter rules of their own.
slides.3.title: A short history
slides.3.highlights.0.title: The Dutch traders story
slides.3.highlights.0.content: The popular account: Dutch traders came to the Cognac area for salt, wood and wine; wine travelled badly, so they distilled it into eau-de-vie, and a second distillation made it finer (intowine, a retold popular account)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Armagnac's ancient record
slides.3.highlights.1.content: alcademics: the oldest known Armagnac production document dates from 1310, about 150 years before Cognac; the AOC was created in 1936 and the BNIA in 1941
slides.3.highlights.2.title: The impact of phylloxera
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Phylloxera hit Armagnac in 1879 and destroyed about half of the vineyards; in Cognac Folle Blanche was likewise displaced by Ugni Blanc (alcademics, Martell)
slides.3.content: Sources vary on historical detail, so only points with a clear source are listed.
